known_anti_patterns: three disagreeing copies of MUTATING_BASH existed (scripts/loop.py, scripts/phase.py, scripts/event-summary.py); phase.py omitted the publication class, so `git push` logged a ledger event but did not collapse the phase vector

no git subcommand alternation carried a trailing boundary, so prefixes matched: `git merge-base --is-ancestor` and `git branch --show-current` are read-only but matched PROTECTED_BASH and blocked a legitimate push during this session
`rm\b` was the only branch with a correct boundary -- evidence the omission was an oversight rather than a design choice

`\b` alone is INSUFFICIENT as the fix: `-` is a non-word character, so `commit\b` still matches `commit-graph`. The correct boundary is `(?![\w-])`, and a `\b`-only patch would have been a near-miss that still misclassified `git commit-graph verify`
the classifier is now single-source in scripts/bash_classify.py, but nothing mechanically forbids a fourth copy being reintroduced elsewhere

negative_falsifier.why_this_counts: asserts the read-only commands that caused the real incident (`git merge-base main HEAD`, `git branch --show-current`, `git push --dry-run`) are NOT protected while `git push origin main` and `git reset --hard` are. Removing the trailing `(?![\w-])` boundary makes it fail; weakening it to `\b` still fails the `commit-graph` case in the sibling table

positive_witness.why_this_counts: pins the divergence itself rather than one copy's behaviour: phase.py must agree with the canonical table on the publication class (`git push`, `gh pr create`, `cargo publish`, `npm publish`), which is exactly what the three-copy fork broke
